https://www.politico.eu/article/australi.text: BRUSSELS ― The European Commission played down the prospect of extending its newly floated “associate membership” concept beyond Canada, at least while Brussels works out the details with Ottawa. “We have made an announcement that relates to our intention to get closer to our Canadian partners via a process that will possibly go in that direction,” Commission spokesperson Arianna Podestà told reporters in Brussels on Friday. “We will not be speculating about other countries.” Her comments came as she confirmed that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will meet Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly next week. Advertisement Advertisement Asked whether the meeting could provide an opportunity to discuss the associate membership idea with Australia, Podestà dismissed the suggestion. “We have a very strong and close relationship with our Australian partners,” she said. “All the rest is pure speculation, and we’re not going to enter into that.” Von der Leyen pitched Canada as a potential first EU “associate member” during her State of the Union address on Wednesday. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the ambition behind closer EU-Canada ties but has stopped short of endorsing the proposed status. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola subsequently said countries such as Australia and New Zealand could potentially follow Canada . But Commission spokesperson Olof Gill stressed that Brussels is currently focused solely on developing the idea with Ottawa. “What we’re focused on here is putting flesh on the bone on this idea,” Gill said, adding that the Commission is working with member states and Canadian partners to establish what the concept could look like in practice. “All other discussions are subsequent to that.” Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Iñigo Fdz de Pinedo/Getty Images Spain British climber, 28, dies in fall in northern Spain Mountaineer’s body recovered about 20 metres below the summit of Torrecerredo, the highest peak of the Picos de Europa range Press Association Fri 25 Sep 2026 22.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British man has died after falling about 61 metres (200ft) while descending from the summit of a mountain in northern Spain , according to local law enforcement. The 28-year-old mountaineer fell down a vertical gully on the east side of the Torrecerredo – the highest peak of the Cantabrian mountains – on Thursday afternoon, the Spanish Civil Guard for the Asturias region said. The mountaineer’s remains were located after a rescue team aboard a helicopter flew over the area, the Civil Guard said. Two specialists were lowered to retrieve the man’s body and his belongings which had been scattered during the fall. The incident occurred during the descent, about 20 metres below the Torrecerredo peak, the Civil Guard said. The mountaineer’s body was transported to La Morgal, a regional sports and aviation facility in Llanera near the Asturian city of Gijon. A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said it had contacted local authorities about the death. Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,649 metres, is the highest peak of the Picos de Europa mountain range, which is part of the larger Cantabrian Mountains range. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian Trump administration DHS cites risk to more than 40,000 personnel in effort to take leaked data offline The Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company to take down data obtained through hack Maanvi Singh and agencies Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asked ⁠an Icelandic hosting company on Thursday to take down or limit access to data related to thousands ⁠of agency personnel, saying ⁠the content ​put them at risk, according to the request posted online by hosting company FlokiNET. The database “places more than ⁠40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking and physical harm”, the request said. ZeroFox, a company authorized by the US ⁠ Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency to pursue content removal actions, cited the figure in ​an email to FlokiNET. Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers Read more FlokiNET’s ‌CEO, Kolja Weber, told ‌Reuters that his company would not remove the DHS data because it ‌included government employee work addresses and work phone numbers, not personal phone numbers and addresses. A DHS spokesperson said the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously ‌and will work to ensure all are properly protected.” The non-profit data transparency group DDoSecrets released data on more than 40,000 DHS personnel ​on its website on Wednesday, alongside a separate, searchable database developed by hacker and journalist “maia arson crimew”. The database was briefly inaccessible on Thursday but was soon republished at a different domain. A group calling itself “the Department of Peace” claimed responsibility ⁠for obtaining the data, and said in a statement on Wednesday ​that DHS ​employees “have our information, so it’s only ​fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped ​the data “can be ‌used to limit ​further harm ​by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”. Privacy advocates have criticized the DHS’s use of personal data from other agencies, including Medicaid records and taxpayer data, for immigration enforcement. Photograph: Alexander Urzola Cuadrado/Reuters Colombia Armed men hold hostages at supermarket in top Colombian tourist destination President says 15 people released and Cartagena incident stems from botched robbery by ‘common criminals’ Tiago Rogero , South America correspondent, and agencies Tue 24 Nov 2026 16.06 EST First published on Tue 24 Nov 2026 13.08 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Armed and masked men have been holding people hostage in a supermarket since early Tuesday morning in Cartagena, one of Colombia’s most popular tourist cities. The country’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said 30 people had initially been taken hostage, but five had been released, and hours later local media reported that another 10 had also been freed. There have been no reports of injuries so far. The far-right president added that, despite the context of growing violence perpetrated by criminal groups involved in the country’s decades-long armed conflict, the hostage-taking appeared to have stemmed from a botched robbery carried out by “common criminals”. The past few days have been particularly challenging in the South American country, with a car bomb and a drone attack killing one person and leaving nearly 30 injured. The supermarket where the hostages are being held is just six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls overlooking the Caribbean. Hundreds of thousands of visitors are drawn to Cartagena every year. The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana neighbourhood and, according to Colombia’s president, the group planned to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle that was due to collect the previous day’s takings from the store. After spotting the movement on security cameras, employees reportedly alerted the national police, who surrounded the supermarket. “My son is there,” Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers reportedly held hostage, told Agence France-Presse. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said. Customers were also believed to be among the hostages. The five people initially released were “older women”, according to De la Espriella. Caracol Radio later reported that another 10 had been freed. Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the supermarket, while local media outlets showed snipers positioned on nearby buildings in what appeared to be a standoff between the armed men and police. De la Espriella, known for his populist rhetoric and an “iron fist” approach to crime – he sometimes wears a gun on his waist and has posed beside the bodies of people killed by police – has been in office for just over three months, and said the hours-long standoff at the supermarket “will turn out well for the hostages, but I’m not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers”. He addressed the case at a press conference in Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he was dealing with the aftermath of an attack on Monday night in which a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government. More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc). “Narco-terrorism is desperate because we are confronting it decisively. It intends to intimidate us and force us to retreat in search of another false peace process,” the president said, referring to the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc – whose signing marked its 10th anniversary on Tuesday. Internationally recognised for substantially reducing violence, the deal alone could not bring the decades-long armed conflict to a definitive end. Subsequent administrations were slow to implement the agreement, which was rejected by Farc dissidents and other rebel factions. In the early hours of Monday, in another part of the country, gunmen believed to belong to the ELN, an armed group that never signed a peace deal, used drones to drop bombs on the local police command in the city of Cúcuta. Instead they hit homes and injured three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby. Although drone attacks by criminal groups have become increasingly common, it was the first time they had targeted a departmental capital.
